content: Inocybe is a large and taxonomically complex genus of mushrooms. Members of the genus Inocybe are mycorrhizal, meaning they form symbiotic associations with the roots of trees. Evidence suggests that the high degree of speciation within this genus may be attributed to adaptations to different tree species and possibly to specific local environmental conditions. The mushrooms in this genus typically exhibit various shades of brown, although some species display lilac or purplish hues. The caps of these mushrooms are generally small and conical in shape, though they tend to flatten somewhat as they age. A prominent raised central knob is often present on the cap. The surface of the cap frequently appears fibrous or frayed, which has led to the genus being commonly referred to as fiber caps. Many species within the genus emit a distinctive odor, which has been described as musty or spermatic. Inocybe species are not considered suitable for human consumption. Many of them contain significant amounts of muscarine, a toxic compound, and there is no straightforward method to distinguish these toxic species from potentially edible ones. In fact, Inocybe is one of the most commonly encountered mushroom genera where microscopic examination is required for definitive identification at the species level. Seven species within the genus are known to be hallucinogenic, as they contain the psychoactive compound psilocybin. One such species, Inocybe aeruginascens, also contains aeruginascine (N,N,N-trimethyl-4-phosphoryloxytryptamine). The genus comprises hundreds of species, making it impractical to provide a complete list. However, representative species include: Inocybe adaequata Inocybe aeruginascens (psychoactive) Inocybe coelestium (psychoactive) Inocybe corydalina var. corydalina (psychoactive) Inocybe corydalina var. erinaceomorpha (psychoactive) Inocybe geophylla Inocybe haemacta (psychoactive) Inocybe hystrix Inocybe lacera Inocybe obscura Inocybe rimosa Inocybe patouillardii Inocybe sororia Inocybe tricolor (psychoactive) Inocybe violaceocaulis (previously classified as Inocybe geophylla var. lilacina). In Western Australia, what is now recognized as Inocybe violaceocaulis was previously referred to as Inocybe geophylla var. lilacina by some Australian taxonomists. However, Matheny and Bougher (2005) identified this as a misapplication of the name Inocybe geophylla var. lilacina. In certain countries, such as Papua New Guinea and other underdeveloped regions, Inocybe mushrooms are consumed as food. This practice increases the risk of severe poisoning due to the difficulty in distinguishing edible species from toxic ones within the genus.
